kurz: Why standard valuation does not produce meaningful results for banks, insurers, cyclicals and loss-making companies, and which methods take its place.

bloecke.md:
Every standard valuation assumes a clear separation between operating business and financing. The operating business generates cash flows, and financing distributes these flows between providers of equity and debt. The calculation based on free cash flow and cost of capital rests on this separation.

For four types of company this basis is missing. For banks, debt is the product and not the financing. For insurers, the profit on in-force business only emerges over decades. The reported profit of cyclicals depends essentially on the phase of the cycle, and loss-making companies have no profit at all on which a calculation could be based. In these cases the standard formulas produce meaningless results.

## Banks

For a machinery manufacturer, debt is a financing decision. It could be replaced by equity and the business would remain the same. For a bank, by contrast, debt is part of the business itself. Deposits and borrowed funds are lent on, and interest expense is an operating expense and not a financing item. A net financial debt figure therefore cannot be meaningfully calculated, and consequently neither can an enterprise value. Discounting free cash flow to the firm at the weighted average cost of capital is wrong for a bank from the outset.

Supervision is a further factor. How much a bank can pay out is determined by the regulatory capital requirement and not by free cash flow. If the balance sheet grows, capital has to be retained, even if cash were available. In Germany, a bank's single-entity financial statements follow Sections 340 et seq. HGB (Commercial Code) and the forms of the RechKredV (Accounting Ordinance for Credit Institutions). These have nothing in common with the industrial format of Section 266 HGB, so even the layout does not fit the usual analysis.

Three other methods are viable. The first is free cash flow to equity after meeting the capital requirement, discounted at the cost of equity. The second is the dividend discount model, the third the relationship between price-to-book ratio and return on equity.

bloecke.erklaerung: The relationship is derived from the dividend discount model and is central for financial companies. A price-to-book ratio above 1 is only justified for a bank if its return on equity is above its cost of equity. If return on equity is below it, a P/B below 1 is the mathematically correct result and not a sign of a cheap valuation.
variablen: sustainable return on equity, not the figure from a good year
sustainable growth of balance sheet total and profit
return required by shareholders, usually in double digits for European banks
bloecke.beispiel: With an ROE of 9.75%, a growth rate g of 2% and a cost of equity of 10%, the result is (9.75 − 2) / (10 − 2) = 0.97. The fair P/B is therefore just under one.

bloecke.titel: Price-to-book ratio and return on equity of US sectors
bloecke.unter: The financial sectors lie almost on a straight line, as the formula predicts. Software and the market as a whole lie far above it, because their balance sheet book value does not contain the assets that determine their value.

bloecke.md:
A bank with a sustainable return on equity of 6%, a cost of equity of 10% and 2% growth has a formula value of (6 − 2) / (10 − 2) = 0.5. At a P/B of 0.7 it is therefore expensive rather than cheap.

A second limitation concerns book value. It is only as reliable as the bank's loan loss provisioning. If the loan book has been written down too optimistically, you are valuing equity that does not exist. Third, the screening scores from the previous lesson are expressly unusable here. The Altman Z-score is not intended for banks, insurers and real estate companies, and the Beneish M-score expressly not for financial institutions.

## Insurers

An insurer collects premiums today and pays claims later. In the meantime it manages capital that does not belong to it, known as the float. Its annual result therefore mixes three very different figures: the underwriting result, the investment result and the change in provisions, which is based on an estimate. For a property insurer, the sources of earnings are separated using the combined ratio, that is claims and expenses divided by earned premiums. If it is below 100%, the company already earns money on the insurance business itself. If it is above, it finances underwriting from investment income.

For a life insurer, the annual result is fundamentally unsuitable as a yardstick. A policy with a thirty-year term delivers its profit over thirty years. How much of it becomes visible in a single financial year depends on the accounting and not on the business. Embedded value was developed for this problem.

bloecke.formel: Embedded value = adjusted net asset value + present value of future profits from in-force business − cost of capital
bloecke.erklaerung: Embedded value measures the value of the in-force business, not that of the whole company, because new business is expressly not included. Adding the value of future new business gives the appraisal value. Market-consistent calculations follow the MCEV Principles of the CFO Forum of 2008/2009.
bloecke.beispiel: An insurer with €6 billion of adjusted net assets and a present value of €4 billion from in-force business has an embedded value of €10 billion. If its market value is €12 billion, the market is paying €2 billion for all the new business of the coming decades.

bloecke.md:
Since Solvency II became binding, many European insurers no longer report MCEV. For supervisory purposes, what counts is the market-consistent solvency balance sheet and the solvency ratio, that is eligible own funds divided by the solvency capital requirement (SCR, Section 96 VAG, Insurance Supervision Act; the minimum capital requirement is governed by Section 122 VAG). This ratio is public and comparable. However, it measures an insurer's safety and not its earning power.

For financial reporting, since IFRS 17, which is mandatory for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2023, the contractual service margin has been the more meaningful figure. It shows the profit from in-force business that has not yet been earned, is reported on the balance sheet and is released to profit or loss over the term of the contracts. It thus largely performs the task for which embedded value used to be needed. Alongside this, an insurer's German single-entity financial statements continue to follow Sections 341 et seq. HGB and the RechVersV (Accounting Ordinance for Insurance Undertakings).

bloecke.md:
## Cyclicals

In steel, chemicals, shipping, semiconductors and oil, the margin fluctuates more than revenue. Since profit is the product of the two, it fluctuates many times more. This creates a systematic distortion. At the profit peak the P/E looks low, in the trough it is high or not defined at all. Screening for low P/Es therefore reliably leads to cyclicals being bought at the top.

The countermeasure is normalisation. Instead of the profit in the reference year, you take the average margin over a full cycle and apply it to current revenue. The Shiller CAPE does the same for the market as a whole with ten years of inflation-adjusted earnings. On 18 September 2026 it stood at 40.94; the historical mean is 17.42.

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation for a cyclical company over twelve years
bloecke.unter: Schematic representation of a fictitious company with revenue between €800 million and €1,150 million and a net margin between 1% and 12%. Reported profit varies by a factor of 16, normalised earnings by a factor of 1.4.

bloecke.titel: Two ratios for the same company at a constant market value of €950m

bloecke.md:
The first mistake is too short a period. The average of the last three years is not a normalisation if all three years were in an upswing. A complete cycle is needed. For semiconductors it spans a few years, for oil, shipping and property development more like seven to ten.

The second mistake is a structural break. Normalising assumes that the cycle recurs. If demand shifts permanently, for example in coal-fired power generation, supplying the combustion engine industry or bricks-and-mortar retail, the historical margin is wrong, even if it looks cautious. Before any normalisation, it therefore has to be clarified whether the market will come back or disappear.

## Companies without profits

Here it helps to divide them into three groups, because each requires a different method. A temporary loss, for example at cyclicals in a trough or in restructuring cases, is normalised as above. A structural growth loss arises, for example, at a software company that books sales and development spending as current expenses and therefore reports losses even though the business is scaling. This calls for a sales multiple. However, it only becomes a valuation through an assumed target margin; without one it is just a number.

bloecke.formel: EV / sales = target EBIT margin × EV / EBIT
bloecke.erklaerung: Every sales multiple contains an assumption about the margin and can therefore be checked. Working backwards from the EV/sales paid and a typical EV/EBIT for the sector gives the margin that the share price assumes for the steady state. Numerator and denominator must be consistent. Enterprise value goes with sales, market capitalisation with profit.
bloecke.beispiel: A software company trades at an EV/sales of 12. According to Damodaran data from January 2026, the sector trades at an EV/EBIT of 32.4. The share price therefore assumes a permanent operating margin of 12 / 32.4 = around 37%. This margin is a verifiable assumption.

bloecke.md: The third group covers the extreme case: companies with neither profit nor revenue. Examples are a biotech company with an active ingredient in Phase II or a resource explorer with a deposit but no mine. Here there is no figure to which a multiple could be applied. The individual project is therefore valued, using the risk-adjusted present value. The success case is calculated in full and then weighted by its probability. The costs of the current development phase are incurred in any case and are deducted in full. The costs of later phases only arise if the previous ones succeed and are therefore weighted by the probability of reaching that phase.

bloecke.titel: rNPV of a Phase II programme
bloecke.md:
The model assumes that the present value of the net cash flows in the event of approval is €2,400 million, the present value of the outstanding development and approval costs €300 million and the probability of success from Phase II 15%. For simplicity, all outstanding costs are deducted in full. This is cautious, because the costs of later phases are only incurred if Phase II succeeds.

`rNPV = 0.15 × 2,400 − 300 = 360 − 300 = €60 million`

With a probability of success of 12% instead of 15%, the result is `0.12 × 2,400 − 300 = −€12 million`. A difference of three percentage points in a variable that nobody can observe therefore reverses the sign. Actual success rates vary greatly by indication and phase. Published industry studies put the figure for Phase II in the low double-digit percentage range.

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation of rNPV as a function of the probability of success
bloecke.unter: With the assumptions from the example, the value depends linearly on the probability of success and changes sign at around 12.5%, so a point valuation has no informative value here.

bloecke.md:
For the resource explorer, a second idea comes into play. A deposit behaves like a call option on the commodity price whose exercise price is the extraction cost per unit. That is why a deposit that would be uneconomic to mine at today's prices can have a positive value, namely a time value. For the same reason, explorers' share prices multiply when commodity prices rise. They are equivalent to out-of-the-money options and are therefore maximally leveraged.

The most important risk in practice is dilution and not geology. A company without cash flow finances itself through new shares. An estimate of value per share that does not take into account the capital increases up to production therefore comes out systematically too high.

An explorer has a project present value of €300 million after all investment and currently 100 million shares. Before production starts, it still has to raise €120 million of equity, realistically at a share price of €1.20. This requires 100 million new shares. The new capital pays for the investment that has already been deducted in the project present value and is therefore added to the project present value.

Naive calculation: 300 / 100 = €3.00 per share.
Correct calculation: (300 + 120) / 200 = €2.10 per share.

Dilution therefore costs 30% of the naive valuation. It results from a capital increase that has not yet taken place and does not appear in any ratio.

For companies whose business model makes a total loss a real possibility, Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG (Income Tax Act) must be borne in mind. Under it, losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from the sale of shares, and therefore not against interest, dividends or gains on funds. An investor who mainly holds distributing ETFs and also sells an individual share at a loss may be unable to use this loss for years. This does not argue against such positions. However, the size of the position should not be based on the hoped-for tax effect.

In all four cases the problem lies in the input and not in the formula. For a bank, free cash flow to all providers of capital does not exist even conceptually. For a life insurer, the profit lies outside the reporting period. For a cyclical company, the phase of the cycle in which the year happens to fall determines the annual profit. For a loss-making company, the denominator is missing altogether. Before any valuation, the question to settle is therefore less the choice of model than whether the figure used is a reliable measure of the business.

mitnehmen: For banks and insurers, debt is part of the business and not of the financing, so FCFF and WACC are by definition not applicable there; they are replaced by FCFE, dividend discounting and the relationship P/B = (ROE − g) / (cost of equity − g).
A P/B below 1 can only be assessed together with the corresponding return on equity; if ROE is below the cost of equity, it is the mathematically correct value.

Cyclicals look cheap precisely when their profits are at their peak; normalisation therefore uses the average margin over a full cycle instead of the last three years, and only where the cycle recurs.
Every sales multiple contains a margin assumption; EV/sales divided by a typical EV/EBIT for the sector gives the target margin implied by the share price and makes it verifiable.
Where there is neither profit nor revenue, projects are valued using rNPV and viewed as options; future dilution often costs more value than any assumption about the project itself.

begriffe.text: Market value divided by balance sheet equity. For financial companies the P/B is the central valuation measure, because approximately P/B = (ROE − g) / (cost of equity − g) holds. Without the corresponding return on equity, a P/B cannot be interpreted.

Value of an insurer's existing portfolio of policies, calculated as adjusted net asset value plus the present value of future profits from contracts already concluded, less the cost of capital. New business is not included. Together with new business, the result is the appraisal value.

Claims and expenses of a property or casualty insurer divided by earned premiums. Below 100%, the insurance business is profitable in its own right; above that, underwriting is cross-subsidised from investment income.

Profit that results from applying the average margin of a complete business cycle to current revenue. It corrects the distortion that makes cyclicals look cheap at the profit peak and expensive in the trough.

Risk-adjusted present value. Each cash flow is weighted by the probability that it will occur: the present value of the success case by the probability of success, and the costs of later development phases by the probability of reaching those phases. The method is standard for valuing individual biotech and exploration projects.
